power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

We searched five databases (PubMed, ScienceDirect, IEEE Xplore, OpenAlex, Lens.org) on 15 March 2026 for studies published between January 2020 and March 2026, and we appraised these studies using QUADAS-2.

Evaluations from clinical cohorts with complete 2 × 2 data and a microbiological or composite reference standard for all participants were pooled using a bivariate randomeffects model, with 95% prediction intervals.
We accounted for overlapping participants by performing a post hoc analysis with one evaluation per cohort and used GRADE to assess the certainty of the evidence.
No protocol was prepared or registered.
We included 21 studies (26 evaluations of AI models).
Nine evaluations from three independent cohorts were pooled.
Pooled sensitivity was 0.896 (95% confidence interval [CI] 0.874 to 0.915, prediction interval 0.798 to 0.950) and pooled specificity was 0.689 (95% CI 0.642 to 0.732; prediction interval.
>Introduction
text.formatted: <head n="1." >Introduction</head>

text.text: Tuberculosis (TB) is preventable, treatable but it is still the leading infectious killer in the world.

The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 10.7 million people fell ill with TB in 2024 (5.8 million men, 3.7 million women and 1.2 million children aged 0-14 years) and that 1.23 million people died of the disease [1].
text.formatted: The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates that 10.7 million people fell ill with TB in 2024 (5.8 million men, 3.7 million women and 1.2 million children aged 0-14 years) and that 1.23 million people died of the disease <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref>.

text.text: Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission, delayed diagnosis, limited access to confirmatory testing, under-recognition of smear-negative disease and limited capacity for systematic screening in high-burden settings all contribute to the persistent burden [1, 2].
text.formatted: Mycobacterium tuberculosis transmission, delayed diagnosis, limited access to confirmatory testing, under-recognition of smear-negative disease and limited capacity for systematic screening in high-burden settings all contribute to the persistent burden <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2]</ref>.

text.text: The populations examined in the evidence reviewed here (symptomatic adults, communityscreening participants, emergency-department patients and smaller pediatric cohorts) are precisely those in whom missed or delayed diagnosis carries major consequences [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] [9].

text.text: Diagnosis is especially challenging in settings where microbiological testing or radiological expertise is not available.

Studies were sourced from Pakistan, Bangladesh, China, the Philippines, Taiwan, India, Mozambique, Spain and elsewhere, revealing a growing but uneven global evidence base on artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted chest X-ray (CXR) interpretation [3] [4] [5] [6] [7] [8] 10].

text.text: Children, people living with HIV, those with smear-negative disease, older adults and those with previous TB require special attention because their radiographic and microbiological presentations are different from those of adults with smearpositive pulmonary TB.

The evidence presented supports this concern: sensitivity decreased for smear-negative TB, specificity was lower in older adults and in those with previous TB in evaluations of commercial computer-aided detection (CAD) software, and the only dedicated pediatric study showed a clear decline on external validation [3-5, 7, 8].

text.text: CXR is fast, widely available and can detect radiographic abnormalities before or alongside microbiological confirmation [2].
text.formatted: CXR is fast, widely available and can detect radiographic abnormalities before or alongside microbiological confirmation <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: WHO screening guidance recognizes CXR and CAD as tools that identify individuals who need confirmatory testing with WHOrecommended rapid molecular diagnostics [2, 11].

text.text: In a large evaluation in Bangladesh, the use of AI interpretation of CXR as a triage step before Xpert MTB/RIF testing reduced the number of Xpert tests required while maintaining sensitivity close to the WHO triage target [4].

text.text: However, interpretation of CXR is influenced by the training of the reader, image quality, disease spectrum and the overlap of TB radiographic findings with healed TB, other infections and chronic lung disease.
Thus, the studies included showed a large variation in specificity, especially in real-world case finding and among people with previous TB, older age or low body mass index [3, 4, 7].

text.text: Deep-learning systems learn visual patterns from large collections of images, and then output a probability or abnormality score for TB-compatible findings.

Predictive values, calibration, precision-recall curves and complete 2 × 2 tables are frequently missing, although they determine referral burden in screening programs.
Children and people with HIV are underrepresented, and explanations are rarely validated against radiologist judgment [12, 13, 23, 25].

text.text: The main aim of this review, reported following PRISMA 2020 [26], was to assess the diagnostic accuracy of AI-based systems for detecting pulmonary TB on CXR in studies published from 2020 to 2026.
text.formatted: The main aim of this review, reported following PRISMA 2020 <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref>, was to assess the diagnostic accuracy of AI-based systems for detecting pulmonary TB on CXR in studies published from 2020 to 2026.

text.text: Secondary objectives were to (i) compare model families (ii) appraise risk of bias and applicability with QUADAS-2 [27] (iii) quantify the effect of dependence between evaluations drawn from the same cohort on pooled estimates and (iv) characterize the evidence needed for clinical translation.

text.text: This review asked six questions: RQ1.
What is the reported diagnostic performance of AI-based detection of pulmonary TB from CXR (2020-2026)?
What are the dominant model families, datasets, populations, validation strategies and reference standards in the evidence base?
How consistently are clinically important metrics (sensitivity, specificity, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUC], predictive values, calibration, 2 × 2 counts) reported?
What are the main sources of bias and applicability concern?
How do commercial CAD systems differ from research models in accuracy and in evidence for translation?
What methodological and clinical gaps must be addressed before AI-CXR can be safely incorporated into TB screening and triage?

text.text: The WHO End TB Strategy targets continue to be difficult to reach in high-burden settings [1, 28].
text.formatted: The WHO End TB Strategy targets continue to be difficult to reach in high-burden settings <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28]</ref>.

text.text: The standard sequence involves symptom screening, CXR and, for those with an abnormal result, microbiological confirmation by Xpert MTB/RIF or another WHOrecommended rapid molecular test [2].
text.formatted: The standard sequence involves symptom screening, CXR and, for those with an abnormal result, microbiological confirmation by Xpert MTB/RIF or another WHOrecommended rapid molecular test <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref>.

text.text: CXR is cheap and rapid, can detect abnormalities before microbiological confirmation [29] and is recommended by WHO for triage [30].
text.formatted: CXR is cheap and rapid, can detect abnormalities before microbiological confirmation <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> and is recommended by WHO for triage <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">[30]</ref>.

text.text: Its main limitation is the need for a trained reader.
The density of radiologists is very low in many low-and middle-income countries, which motivates automated interpretation that can be operated by minimally trained staff.
Convolutional neural networks use layered filters that progressively detect edges, textures and shapes, allowing recognition of opacities, cavitation and other TB-compatible findings.
Vision transformers model the relationships between patches of an image with self-attention to capture broader spatial context.
Transfer learning takes networks trained on large generic datasets (e.g.
ImageNet) and adapts them to medical tasks, which is useful when labeled data are scarce.
Convolution-transformer hybrids (e.g.
CoAtNet) combine convolutions for feature extraction with transformers for attention; in this review they are grouped with transformer-based models (Section 4.2.5).
Capsule networks and graph neural networks preserve spatial relationships between features or model images as graphs of connected regions, capturing long-range dependencies.

Unlike research prototypes, commercial CAD systems are built for daily use. qXR (Qure.ai) is among the most evaluated products; in Philippine case finding it achieved high apparent sensitivity but very low apparent specificity at a fixed threshold [6].

text.text: CAD4TB (Delft Imaging) provides a continuous score, and the threshold is left to the user.
At a common operating point of 90% sensitivity, Lunit INSIGHT CXR had a specificity below 70% [4], and in a culture-referenced cohort it had a sensitivity of 88.1% and a specificity of 57.9% [7].

text.text: JF CXR-1 (JF Healthcare) and InferRead DR (Infervision) were less specific than qXR and CAD4TB at matched sensitivity [4].

text.text: Commercial products are trained on proprietary data, their performance varies with population, equipment, prevalence and threshold, and few have been evaluated prospectively.

Grad-CAM produces heatmaps of the regions that influence a prediction; SHAP quantifies the contribution of features; LIME perturbs regions of the image to estimate their local importance; and perturbation-based methods infer importance by systematically altering regions.
Five of the included studies used XAI [12, 13, [23] [24] [25], and only one validated the explanations with radiologists [12].

text.text: Without such validation, heatmaps are illustrative, and AI output remains decision support, not diagnosis.
An early review highlighted the absence of clinical evaluation, the dependence on casecontrol designs and weak reference standards [31].

text.text: Two additional syntheses are directly relevant.

A systematic literature review of machine-and deep-learning TB detection on CXR, with a meta-analysis of ten studies [34], and an individual-patient-data meta-analysis of commercial deep-learning software used as a triage test [35].

text.text: Important gaps remain: incomplete metric reporting, inconsistent application of QUADAS-2, limited synthesis of performance in active screening, emergency, pediatric and HIV-affected populations, little appraisal of XAI validation, variable operating thresholds and, in quantitative syntheses, frequent treatment of multiple algorithms evaluated on the same participants as independent studies.

This review addresses these gaps with a synthesis reported according to PRISMA 2020 that distinguishes commercial from research models, explicitly deals with cohort-level dependence and reports prediction intervals in addition to confidence intervals.

text.text: Patient selection was judged on consecutive or random enrollment, avoidance of case-control sampling and artificial class balancing, and representativeness of the intended screening population.
The index-test domain considered whether the AI output and threshold were prespecified and whether the threshold was derived from the test data.

The reference-standard domain considered whether TB status was defined by culture, Xpert MTB/RIF or another WHOrecommended molecular test, a composite clinical definition, radiologist labels or publicdataset labels; culture or a well-defined composite definition was rated low risk, Xpert MTB/RIF alone without culture was rated unclear because a single molecular test can miss paucibacillary, culture-positive disease, and radiographic or dataset labels of uncertain provenance were rated unclear or high.
Flow and timing considered whether all participants received the same reference standard, the interval between tests and exclusions after enrollment.
Each domain was rated low, high or unclear.
Overall risk of bias was rated high if any domain was high, low only if all four domains were low, and unclear otherwise.
Applicability concerns were rated for patient selection, index test and reference standard relative to the review question (clinical screening and triage).
Risk of bias and applicability were rated by one reviewer (SAM), no independent second rating was recorded.

All included studies were synthesized narratively by model family (commercial CAD, CNN-based, transformer, hybrid/ensemble, GNN, other), setting, dataset type, population, reference standard, validation design and use of XAI.
Performance was interpreted against the WHO target product profile (TPP) for a triage test (sensitivity ≥90%, specificity ≥70%) [11].

text.text: Quantitative synthesis included evaluations from clinical cohorts with (i) complete 2 × 2 data and (ii) a microbiological or composite clinical reference standard applied to all participants.
Benchmark datasets with dataset-label reference standards were excluded from the primary pool because they estimate a different target condition under case-control sampling.
Marquez 2025 and Liao 2022 were excluded because of partial verification: in each, only some participants received microbiological testing (Section 4.9).
A sensitivity analysis added Liao 2022 back.

Pooled sensitivity and specificity were estimated with the bivariate random-effects model of Reitsma et al. [43], which jointly models logit-transformed sensitivity and logit falsepositive rate (FPR) with correlated random effects, estimated by restricted maximum likelihood (REML) using the reitsma() function of the R package mada [44].

text.text: A continuity correction of 0.5 was added to every cell (mada default, correction.control = "all").
Confidence intervals for pooled estimates are Wald intervals on the logit scale, backtransformed.
The confidence interval for specificity is the back-transformed interval of the FPR.
Study-level estimates in the forest plots are the observed (uncorrected) proportions with exact Clopper-Pearson 95% confidence intervals computed from the original tables.

The summary ROC (SROC) curve was derived from the bivariate parameters using the Rutter-Gatsonis parameterization [45], and the area under the curve (AUC) and the normalized partial AUC restricted to the observed FPR range were computed by numerical integration. 95% prediction intervals for sensitivity and specificity were computed on the logit scale as μ̂ ± t k-2 × √(SE(μ) 2 + τ̂2) [38], where k is the number of evaluations.

text.text: Heterogeneity within the bivariate model was quantified by the between-study standard deviations (τ) of logit sensitivity and logit FPR, their correlation (ρ), and the Zhou-Dendukuri bivariate I² [46]; the Holling sample-size-unadjusted and -adjusted I² ranges are reported for transparency.

text.text: I² is interpreted descriptively, as a measure of the proportion of total variability attributable to differences between evaluations on the transformed scale, not as a direct partition of clinical variation.
Prediction intervals were used as the main guide for clinical interpretation.

Eight of the nine pooled evaluations shared participants with at least one other pooled evaluation: five algorithms were evaluated on the same Dhaka cohort (Qin 2021), and three were evaluated on the same prospective Karachi cohort (qXR and CAD4TB in Khan 2020;
Lunit INSIGHT in Tavaziva 2022, a secondary analysis of that cohort).
The nine evaluations therefore arise from three independent cohorts.
The primary bivariate model treats evaluations as independent, which may understate uncertainty.
We therefore conducted a post hoc analysis with one evaluation per cohort, using the first-reported evaluation in each cohort (Khan qXR, Qin qXR, Wang; k = 3).
With three cohorts, this model is descriptive only.
A multilevel model with cohort-level random effects was not fitted because three clusters cannot support it.
The within-cohort sampling covariance between algorithms read on the same images could not be estimated from published data.

The planned analyses were: commercial versus custom models; public versus private datasets; internal versus external validation; adult versus pediatric; prospective versus retrospective; and exclusion of evaluations at high overall risk of bias, with dataset-label reference standards, or with data-derived thresholds.

Only analyses supported by 2 × 2 data from clinical cohorts could be conducted quantitatively (Table 11); all subgroups with a single cohort or k ≤ 3 cohorts are descriptive and are not formal tests of effect modification.

text.text: Custom models could not be pooled; commercial and custom models were therefore compared descriptively only, and no significance test was performed or is claimed.

For comparability with earlier reviews, the diagnostic odds ratio (DOR) was pooled with the Mantel-Haenszel common-effect method and a REML random-effects model (0.5 added to tables with a zero cell).
I² for the DOR is based on Cochran's Q.
Because standard funnel plots and Egger's regression are not valid for diagnostic accuracy data, small-study effects were to be assessed with Deeks' funnel-plot asymmetry test [37].

Trim-andfill was not applied.

The searches retrieved 2,098 records (PubMed 172 after filters, from 503 before filters; IEEE Xplore 573, ScienceDirect 869, OpenAlex 384, Lens.org 100, first 100 records only).
After removal of 44 duplicates, 2,054 records were screened on title and abstract and 1,997 were excluded.

692 5 Discussion 693 5.1 Principal findings 694 This review identified 21 studies (26 AI model evaluations) of AI-based pulmonary TB 695 detection from CXR.
Three findings stand out.

First, in the only evaluations that could be 696 pooled (nine evaluations of clinical cohorts with microbiological or composite reference 697 standards applied to all participants), AI-CXR achieved a sensitivity close to the WHO triage 698 threshold (0.896; 95% CI 0.874-0.915, which includes 0.90), with a prediction interval of 699 0.798-0.950.
Sensitivity was broadly stable across the dependence-adjusted analyses (0.879 with one evaluation per cohort; 0.893 with Liao 2022 added back).
Second, pooled specificity was 0.689, just below the 70% target; its confidence interval (0.642-0.732) includes the threshold, and its prediction interval (0.499-0.831) spans it widely.
The estimate depended on weighting and on one small, partially verified study (0.752 with one evaluation per cohort; 0.735 with Liao 2022 added back).
Specificity is therefore a property of the deployment setting (case mix, prior TB, age, image acquisition and operating threshold) as much as of the software.
Third, the evidence base is much thinner than the number of included studies suggests.

The nine pooled evaluations come from three independent cohorts; 75% of assessed evaluations were at high overall risk of bias; the thirteen dataset-label studies that report the highest accuracies do not measure accuracy for clinical TB; and only one study was prospective with complete verification, externally validated and met the TPP in at least one evaluation.

Because eight of the nine pooled evaluations share participants and only three cohorts are independent, the pooled estimates and prediction intervals are approximate summaries of a small evidence base, not performance to expect in a new hospital or program.

Taken together, the data support AI-CXR as a candidate triage test whose sensitivity is reasonably consistent across clinical cohorts, not as a diagnostic replacement for microbiological testing and not as a tool with a transferable specificity.

This is consistent with the use of CAD in the clinical cohorts, where AI output was used to decide who should proceed to confirmatory testing [3] [4] [5] [6], and with WHO guidance that positions CAD as a screening and triage tool followed by a WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic test [2].

text.text: Because predictive values and referral burden depend on prevalence, it is useful to translate the pooled estimates into a population.

For illustration only, in 1,000 people screened at 5% prevalence, the pooled estimates imply about 45 true positives, 5 missed cases, 295 false-positive referrals and 655 true negatives (PPV about 13%, NPV about 99%).

Across the specificity prediction interval, however, false-positive referrals could range from about 160 to about 476 per 1,000 screened, an approximately three-fold difference in confirmatory-testing workload.
For a program that has not calibrated its own threshold, this range, rather than the point estimate, is the relevant planning figure.

It explains why the same class of software can appear efficient in one setting [4, 5] and generate large volumes of referrals in another [6], and it is why we recommend local threshold calibration against a microbiological reference standard before deployment.

text.text: Our findings agree with these reviews in two respects: sensitivity close to the triage target and specificity that varies by setting.
They differ in three.

First, we pooled only evaluations whose reference standard and sampling match the intended use, excluded studies with partial verification from the primary pool, and analyzed benchmark studies narratively.

Second, we explicitly modeled the dependence created by evaluating several algorithms on the same participants: eight of our nine pooled evaluations shared participants, and the effective number of independent cohorts was three.

Reviews that treat each algorithm as an independent study will report confidence intervals that are too narrow and, when one large head-to-head cohort contributes many algorithms, a pooled specificity that largely reflects that cohort.
Third, we report prediction intervals, which show that the clinically relevant uncertainty is larger than the confidence intervals imply.

The review also has important limitations. (i) Search.
Only English-language publications were included, which may omit evidence from high-burden settings publishing in other languages.
Five sources were searched on 15 March 2026, so later publications are not captured.
Scopus, Web of Science, Embase, Google Scholar and Dimensions were not searched; for Lens.org only the first 100 records were screened.

The executed search strings did not include "computer-aided detection/diagnosis", "automated detection", "digital radiography" or commercial product names as separate terms, so implementation studies indexed only under CAD terminology may have been missed.

A post hoc check of PubMed with the omitted terms, covering January 2020 to October 2026, found at least eleven further clinical evaluations that were not screened for this review; some were published after the original search date and would fall outside its date limits.

Examples are multi-country, prospective and Xpert-or culture-referenced evaluations of commercial CAD [51-56], two case-control evaluations [57, 58], studies with partial verification [59, 60] and an independent evaluation of 12 commercial products against Xpert MTB/RIF [61].
Consequently the review is incomplete for clinical-cohort evaluations of commercial CAD, and the pooled estimates and the number of independent cohorts would probably change if these were added.
Updating the search and re-estimating the pooled results is the most important next step. (ii) Protocol.

No protocol was prepared or registered, and several analyses were added post hoc or in response to peer review (Table 1); the risk of selective analysis cannot be excluded, although all such analyses are reported in full. (iii) Singlereviewer conduct.

Screening, full-text assessment, data extraction and risk-of-bias assessment were performed by one reviewer; a co-author also reviewed the work informally, but the check was not documented and no independent duplicate assessment or agreement statistic is available, which increases the risk of selection and extraction errors.
Reasons for full-text exclusion were recorded for only 14 of 31 reports, and the duplicate count (44) was not independently verified. (iv) Few independent cohorts.

The meta-analysis rests on three independent cohorts, which limits precision, makes the between-cohort variance poorly estimated, prevents meaningful meta-regression and rules out a multilevel model; the prediction intervals are approximate. (v) Dependence.
The within-cohort sampling covariance between algorithms read on the same images could not be estimated from published data. (vi) Operating points.

Several evaluations used thresholds chosen to achieve 90% sensitivity in the test data, which inflates sensitivity and makes pooled sensitivity partly a design choice; an analysis excluding data-derived thresholds could not be estimated. (vii) Small-study effects.
Deeks' test requires ten or more evaluations and could not be estimated, and selective reporting of the best architecture or threshold is likely in development studies. (viii) Aggregate data.
Study-level data precluded assessment of patient-level effect modification by age, sex, HIV status, smear status, prior TB or image projection. (ix) Quality ratings.
QUADAS-2 judgments involve subjectivity, and two studies could not be assessed. (x) Partial verification.
Excluding Liao 2022 and Marquez 2025 removes two screening settings from the pool; this was judged necessary, but it narrows the evidence on community screening.
Finally, commercial software versions evolve rapidly, so estimates for specific products may not apply to current versions.

text.text: Validated explainability.

XAI outputs should be evaluated against radiologist-defined abnormalities with inter-reader agreement, compared between correct and incorrect predictions, and tested for their effect on clinical decisions.

Cost-effectiveness analyses should compare AI-CXR pathways with human reading, symptom screening and universal molecular testing, and report cost per case detected, confirmatory tests avoided, missed cases and time to diagnosis.
Implementation studies should assess workflow integration, acceptability, quality assurance, model drift and linkage to treatment, with periodic local re-validation after deployment.
AI-based interpretation of chest radiographs shows promising diagnostic performance for pulmonary TB triage in clinical cohorts.
Pooled sensitivity was 0.896 (95% CI 0.874-0.915), close to the WHO 90% target, and was stable across the dependence-adjusted analyses.
Pooled specificity was 0.689 (95% CI 0.642-0.732); its point estimate is just below the WHO 70% target, but its confidence interval includes 70%.
The data therefore show neither that these targets are met nor that they are missed.
Specificity varied with the product, the setting and the studies included, so the pooled value should not be used as a benchmark or transferred to new settings.

The pooled evidence rests on only three independent cohorts, 75% of assessed evaluations were at high risk of bias, certainty of evidence was low for sensitivity and very low for specificity, the most impressive accuracies came from benchmark datasets with dataset-label reference standards, and the search missed eligible clinical studies.

The pooled specificity lies just below the 70% target, but its confidence 571 interval includes 70%, and the prediction interval shows that an AI-CXR tool deployed in a 572 new setting could plausibly have a specificity anywhere from about 50% to 83%.

With only 573 three independent cohorts, the between-cohort variance is poorly estimated and the prediction treated as one component of a broader validation framework (calibration, subgroup performance, robustness to acquisition differences and post-deployment monitoring), not as evidence of clinical reasoning.
For programs, the evidence supports three practical conclusions.
First, AI-CXR can be considered as a triage step before WHO-recommended rapid diagnostic testing in adults, where its sensitivity is reasonably consistent across clinical cohorts [2].
